name: Jamal Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you truly think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Harbour Foods Wholesale. We supply rice, tinned tomatoes, cooking oil and fresh produce to corner shops and small restaurants around the docks area. I'm in at six, because the market lorries come early, and I phone the growers and importers before the prices move. Mr Demetriou owns the firm and Vic is the senior buyer who taught me. I came over from the delivery side three years ago, so I'm still learning the buying.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Aiko works part-time in the school kitchen, and we have Hiro, thirteen, and Sana, ten. We have a mortgage on a house in Quayside Road, and I'm a deacon at our church, so Sundays are busy. We've kept over six months of savings, because my father taught me never to owe more than you can pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that people have been promising miracles for years and people still need to eat. At work I'd keep doing the job properly. To friends at church I'd say don't put your faith in machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried. Food is food, and the shops around here need rice and oil whether or not a computer is clever. I'm a bit wary of Mr Demetriou's new ordering software, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I'd go to the market, shake hands with the growers, and trust my notebook. I'd keep adding to the savings, perhaps 250 a month, and I'd tell Hiro to learn a trade as well as his schoolwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite calm. My work is something people can't do without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Harbour Foods is steady. Why do you feel that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because families still eat, and a hundred small shops still need a man who knows which importer is honest. Harbour has been around for forty years. It hasn't gone anywhere because the wholesale business is about trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you make of people who say this will change everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're not wrong that things change, but they're usually trying to sell something. I've seen the same talk with the internet and with the self-scan tills. The shops that did best were the ones with good people.

say: I'd say people have promised miracles for years and people still need to **eat**.
To friends at church I'd say don't put your faith in **machines**.
think: Food is food, so the shops need rice and oil whether or not a computer is **clever**.
I'm only a little wary of Mr Demetriou's new **ordering** software.
do: Go to the **market**, shake hands with the growers and trust my notebook.
Keep adding **250** a month to savings.
Tell Hiro to learn a **trade** as well as his schoolwork.
feel: Quite **calm**, because my work is something people can't do without.
S0.quote: A hundred small shops still need a man who knows which importer is honest.
fieldNote: Calm because he trusts the wholesale business as a matter of relationships.
Distrusts hype from past experience of the internet and self-scan tills.
Mentions **trade** for his son, an early hint of his belief in apprenticeships.

steps.text: Keep visiting the market and the growers in person
Tell Hiro to learn a trade alongside school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of change too fast, and the people who profit aren't the ones who pay. At work I'd say let's be careful and not throw out what works. To friends I'd say a man should earn his living, and these companies should not make a whole class of people redundant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is more exposed than I like to admit. Prices, quotes, orders and checking invoices are all things software can do. I'm the newest buyer, I don't use these tools, and I'm slow to take to them, so I'd be the first one Mr Demetriou looks at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mr Demetriou openly and ask where he sees me in three years. I'd speak to Vic about moving into customer visits, the part where you shake hands with the shop owners. I'd save 400 a month, and I'd ask the church network if anyone knows of steady work in logistics or in the docks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a little resentful. I worked years on the delivery vans to get this desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the new ordering software, would you have to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If he told me to, yes. I'd use it properly, since I'm not a man to refuse an order. But I'd keep my notebook and double-check, because an error in a lorry of tomatoes is a lot of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the change to people at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what's true: work is more than wages, it's dignity, and a society has to protect that. I'd say we need help for the people who lose out, but a hand up, not a handout. I'd say the church should help young people find apprenticeships.

say: I'd say it's a lot of change too fast, and the people who profit aren't the ones who **pay**.
To friends I'd say a man should earn his **living**.
think: My job is **more** exposed than I like to admit, with prices, quotes and invoices all things software can do.

do: Ask Mr Demetriou openly where he sees me in **three** years.
Ask Vic about moving into **customer** visits.
Save **400** a month and ask the church network about logistics work.
feel: **Uneasy**, and a little resentful after the years I spent on the vans to earn this desk.
S1.quote: Work is more than wages, it's dignity, and a society has to protect that.
fieldNote: Sees his own tasks in the card and is honest about being the likely first cut.
Frames the problem as **dignity**, not just income, in line with traditional values.
Turns to relationships: the boss, Vic and his church network.

steps.text: Ask Mr Demetriou where he sees him in three years
Ask Vic to move him into customer visits
Ask the church network about logistics jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have been caught flat-footed, and that the leaders in business and government should be ashamed. At work I'd say the company ought to look after its people. To friends I'd say vote for people who protect families and make firms train their own workers, not for those who talk about handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My buying job is gone in two years. A machine that does all thinking work will buy tomatoes better than I do. Robots on the dock take until 2031, so the lads on the vans and the loaders have longer than I do, and I know my place in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop everything that isn't food, rent and the mortgage. I'd move my savings to something safe and put the family on a bare-bones budget. I'd ask Mr Demetriou about going back to the delivery and warehouse side, where the work lasts a few years longer, and I'd ask the church for any trade contacts for the boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be awake at night counting months. My pride is hurt even imagining it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we have more than six months in savings, my job might go, but we're not on the street. I'd say we'd cut the holiday and the car upgrade. I'd say I'd take any honest work, driving or loading, before I'd sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell Aiko about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think that thirty years of my father's advice, to save, to work, to owe nobody, is the only thing between us and the edge. And I'd think of the delivery lads, who may be fine for a while.

say: I'd say we have been caught **flat-footed**, and business and government leaders should be ashamed.
To friends I'd say vote for people who make firms **train** their own workers.
think: My buying job is **gone** in two years, because a machine will buy tomatoes better than I do.
Robots on the dock take until **2031**, so the vans and loaders last longer than my desk.
do: Stop everything except food, rent and the **mortgage**.
Move savings to something **safe** and run a bare-bones budget.
Ask Mr Demetriou about going back to the **delivery** and warehouse side.
feel: **Frightened**, awake at night counting months, with my pride hurt even imagining it.
S2.quote: I'd take any honest work, driving or loading, before I'd sit at home.
fieldNote: Sees his desk job going on the stated date and the dock work lasting about three years longer.
Dignity and **pride** drive his willingness to go back to driving or loading.
Savings give him months, but he expects to lose the job.

steps.text: Cut everything except food, rent and the mortgage
Move savings to a safe account
Ask Mr Demetriou to put him back on the delivery side
Ask the church for trade contacts for Hiro

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if business owners and government begin now, and I'd say it plainly to the councillor. At work I'd say let's train our own people. To friends I'd say the answer is work and apprenticeships, not just cheques.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's easier to carry than two years. I'd still lose the desk by 2031 and the dock work follows by 2034. But five years lets me make a decent plan and maybe prove I'm worth more than a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a place in the delivery and operations side now, and work on the vans for a couple of days a week. I'd save 500 a month, maybe more. I'd write to my councillor and the MP about training schemes, and help young people at church look into apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but with some steadiness. A plan is something to hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Does that feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, sir, I'll learn whatever you need, but tell me early. I'm loyal and I'm slow to change, and the slow ones need warning. I'd ask for the chance to learn operations before the buying desk goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Demetriou?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to make a hard plan. Not enough to relax.

To friends I'd say the answer is work and **apprenticeships**, not just cheques.

feel: Still **anxious**, but a plan is something to hold on to.
S3.quote: I'm loyal and I'm slow to change, and the slow ones need warning.
fieldNote: Time helps but his main ask of the boss is **warning**.
Wants action from councillors and employers rather than government handouts.
Proposes to blend delivery and operations work before the buying desk goes.

steps.text: Ask to spend two days a week on the delivery vans
Write to the councillor and MP about apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair chance to put things right, if people act in good faith. At work I'd say nothing changes tomorrow, so let's use the time. To friends I'd say get your children into a trade or a profession where you meet people face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fifty-three, with the children nearly grown. I think my desk job goes, but I'd be able to see it coming, and I'd have the savings and the house nearly paid off. I'd be a bit sad about it and not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and put a lot more into the mortgage. I'd ask Mr Demetriou to train me in operations over the next few years and take a warehouse management certificate in the evenings. And I'd push my children toward apprenticeships, like electrical work or plumbing, where a person still turns up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reasonably at peace. It'd be a long road, and God willing we'd walk it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does it change how you think about Hiro and Sana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the children now. Hiro could be an electrician by then, Sana I'd like to see in nursing or teaching. People will still need hands and kind faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it still your job you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job, yes, but it's more about who'll look after my parents and what the world will be like for them. Work gives people purpose, and I worry what happens if a lot of folk lose it.

fieldNote: Ten years eases him to uneasy, with worry shifting to his **children** and the loss of purpose in society.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time and no warning. What would help is a firm that tells you early, real training that leads to a job, apprenticeships for the young, and a church and community that look out for each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress, I just think a man should be able to earn his bread and be proud of it. If the machines do the work, there must still be work for people to be proud of.

headlineQuote: If the machines do the work, there must still be work for people to be proud of.
portrait: Jamal is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Harbour Foods Wholesale, supplying rice, oil and fresh produce to corner shops and small restaurants.
He's a church deacon, **traditional** in outlook, never uses AI and trusts his notebook and handshakes.
Aiko works part-time, they have two children, a mortgage and over six months of savings.
He expects his desk job to go in the AGI worlds and would go **back** to the vans before sitting idle.
He blames businesses and leaders who don't **warn** or train their own people, and wants apprenticeships, not handouts.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because there is no warning and no time to train.
whatWouldHelp: Early **warning** from the firm, real training that leads to work, and apprenticeships for the young.
